paragraphs: Nesterov's accelerated gradient method is studied here through its algorithmic stability: how sensitive the learning procedure is to perturbations. The paper asks whether a favorable stability result for convex quadratic objectives extends to the broader family of smooth convex objectives. This matters because a guarantee for one mathematical class need not describe the behavior of the same optimizer on a larger class.

Earlier work established that uniform stability grows quadratically with the number of optimization steps for convex quadratic objectives. It conjectured the same growth for general smooth convex objectives. The authors disprove that extension, showing exponential deterioration with the number of gradient steps for two notions of stability, including uniform stability.

The result identifies a substantial distinction between quadratic objectives and the broader smooth convex setting. It also contrasts with known results for ordinary gradient methods, whose stability typically grows linearly with the number of steps. The finding concerns sensitivity during optimization; it does not establish that every accelerated run exhibits exponential instability.
neurips-2021-algorithmic-instabilities-o.tldr: Nesterov's accelerated method can exhibit exponentially deteriorating stability on smooth convex objectives, disproving a proposed extension of quadratic-objective guarantees.

paragraphs: Deploying neural networks on edge devices involves choosing both a network architecture and the numerical precision used by its computations. Searching these choices together offers flexibility across resource budgets, but creates an enormous search space. Training a shared network that represents many candidate designs can also become unstable when those candidates use different precisions.

The paper introduces BatchQuant, a quantizer designed to support fast, stable training of a compact shared supernet. Its Quantized-for-all approach extends this supernet to mixed-precision candidates, including ultra-low bitwidth choices, without retraining. The reported supernet contains more than 10^76 quantized subnets and takes substantially fewer GPU hours to train than previous methods.

This approach matters because a single training process can support a broad range of architecture and precision choices for hardware-aware search. On ImageNet, the authors report state-of-the-art Top-1 accuracy under a complexity budget below 20 MFLOPs. That finding demonstrates the method's effectiveness in the stated low-complexity setting, alongside its flexibility for selecting candidate networks.
neurips-2021-batchquant-quantized-for-al.tldr: BatchQuant stabilizes shared-supernet training so architecture search can explore vast mixed-precision design spaces without retraining each candidate.

paragraphs: Adapting a large pretrained language model by updating all its weights requires many trainable parameters and a separate model copy for each task. The abstract also identifies instability and poor sample efficiency when training data are scarce. Compacter addresses these costs by adding compact, task-specific weight structures to the pretrained model.

Its construction combines adapters, low-rank optimization, and parameterized hypercomplex multiplication. Each inserted weight matrix is assembled as a sum of Kronecker products, which build larger matrices from smaller factors. These products combine shared weights with rank-one matrices specific to each Compacter layer. This organization lets task adaptation use a small set of trainable components rather than independently learning every entry of a large matrix.

The authors report training only 0.047% of the pretrained model's parameters while matching standard fine-tuning on GLUE. They also report better performance on SuperGLUE and in low-resource settings. These findings support the claimed trade-off: substantially fewer trainable parameters can retain, and in the reported settings improve, downstream task performance.
neurips-2021-compacter-efficient-low-ran.tldr: Compacter uses compact structured adapters to match or exceed standard fine-tuning in reported evaluations while training just 0.047% of model parameters.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation improves a compact student network by transferring information from a stronger teacher. The paper examines whether this transfer can work when teacher and student solve different tasks. Its particular case pairs an image classifier as the teacher with an object detector as the student, extending the usual detector-to-detector setup.

This pairing requires more than improving the detector's ability to recognize object categories. Object detection also requires locating those objects within an image. The authors propose strategies that use the classification teacher to improve both recognition and localization. The central contribution is therefore a transfer framework that makes information from one visual task useful for two aspects of another.

Experiments cover several detectors with different backbone networks. The authors report improvements that surpass the detector-to-detector distillation methods they compare against. These results support the practical value of crossing task boundaries during distillation: a teacher's usefulness need not depend on having exactly the same task as its student.
neurips-2021-distilling-image-classifier.tldr: A classifier-to-detector distillation framework improves both object recognition and localization, outperforming compared detector-to-detector methods.

paragraphs: Federated reinforcement learning lets multiple agents collaborate on a decision-making policy without sharing their raw trajectories. The paper addresses two concerns that can undermine this collaboration: whether learning converges, and whether it remains reliable when some participants fail or act maliciously. Treating both questions together connects the value of cooperation to the reliability of its participants.

The authors propose a framework with a convergence guarantee that tolerates random system failures or adversarial attackers among fewer than half of the participating agents. This threshold is part of the stated guarantee. The framework therefore provides a theoretical basis for learning despite a substantial, but bounded, fraction of unreliable participants.

The analysis also guarantees that sample efficiency improves as the number of agents increases while accounting for failures or attacks. In other words, the benefit of adding collaborators is supported alongside the robustness claim. Experiments on several reinforcement learning benchmarks empirically verify the theoretical results, linking the mathematical analysis to observed learning behavior.
neurips-2021-fault-tolerant-federated-re.tldr: The proposed federated reinforcement learning framework guarantees convergence and improving sample efficiency while tolerating fewer than half of agents failing or attacking.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much data average-reward reinforcement learning algorithms need to achieve useful accuracy. It covers two settings: evaluating a policy with TD(lambda) and linear function approximation, and finding an optimal policy with tabular Q-learning. The guarantees concern finite samples and accommodate both constant and diminishing learning step sizes.

A central obstacle is that adding a constant to the value function does not change the relevant solution. This ambiguity prevents the associated Bellman operators from being contractions under any norm, removing a familiar route to convergence analysis. For TD(lambda), the authors work within a carefully chosen subspace where the solution becomes unique.

For Q-learning, the analysis instead uses contraction in a span seminorm, which handles the additive-constant ambiguity. The authors construct a new Lyapunov function using a generalized Moreau envelope and a set indicator through infimal convolution. These mathematical devices support sample-complexity guarantees in a setting where the usual norm-based contraction argument does not apply.
neurips-2021-finite-sample-analysis-of-a.tldr: The paper establishes finite-sample guarantees for average-reward TD(lambda) and tabular Q-learning by handling value functions' additive-constant ambiguity.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings represent entities as points in a mathematical space. Hyperbolic space can represent tree-like hierarchies effectively because its available space grows exponentially. The paper asks how that same geometric property affects generalization when learning from practical data, extending a theoretical comparison previously restricted to idealized noiseless settings.

The authors derive a generalization-error bound covering linear and hyperbolic embeddings under various negative-sampling setups. In this bound, dependence on the embedding space's radius is polynomial for linear space and exponential for hyperbolic space. The geometry that helps represent hierarchies can therefore also increase the statistical burden reflected by the bound.

The analysis uses a bias-variance trade-off to identify a data-size condition under which hyperbolic embeddings can represent a tree better than Euclidean embeddings. It also shows that an imbalanced data distribution can worsen the error bound. The resulting comparison makes the choice of geometry depend on both representational fit and the amount and distribution of available data.
neurips-2021-generalization-bounds-for-g.tldr: Generalization bounds reveal a trade-off between hyperbolic embeddings' ability to represent trees and their stronger radius-dependent statistical cost.

paragraphs: A neural network can reduce cross-entropy loss by learning only some of the features that predict the target. Other useful features may remain undiscovered even though they are present in the training data. The paper calls this phenomenon gradient starvation and studies it in over-parameterized networks trained by gradient descent.

The authors use dynamical systems tools to explain how feature-learning processes become imbalanced during optimization. They identify properties of the learning dynamics that produce this effect and prove that it can be expected under certain statistical structures in the training data. The claim therefore links selective feature learning to both optimization behavior and the structure of the examples.

Building on this formal account, the paper develops a regularization method intended to decouple feature-learning dynamics, together with guarantees for it. The method aims to improve accuracy and robustness in cases affected by gradient starvation. Experiments on simple and real-world out-of-distribution generalization problems illustrate the analysis and the proposed response to this particular learning failure.
neurips-2021-gradient-starvation-a-learn.tldr: Gradient starvation explains how learning some predictive features can suppress others, motivating regularization that decouples their learning dynamics.

paragraphs: An observed network records which pairs of vertices are connected, but network analysis may require estimating the probabilities behind those observed connections. Many existing estimators impose structural assumptions on the network. This paper develops a neighborhood-averaging approach intended to estimate connection probabilities without making strong assumptions about that structure.

The method starts either from a random initialization or from an existing estimate. It then repeatedly updates distances between vertices, identifies sets of similar vertices, and revises connection probabilities. These quantities are refined together, so the current estimate helps determine which vertices should contribute to the next averaging step.

A two-stage neighborhood-selection procedure balances smooth estimates against the ability to preserve local structure. Cross-validation can select the tuning parameters, making the balance adjustable from data. The authors establish theoretical properties and compare the method with existing approaches in simulations and real-data analyses, reporting superior performance. The contribution combines iterative refinement with an explicit mechanism for managing the tension between averaging and local detail.
neurips-2021-iterative-connecting-probab.tldr: An iterative neighborhood-averaging method estimates network connection probabilities while balancing smoothness and preservation of local structure.

paragraphs: Graph-learning theory often assumes that a model observes the entire input graph. That assumption becomes difficult to use when graphs are too large to process conveniently. This paper develops a theoretical framework for graph classification from partial observations, specifically sampled subgraphs, so that the analysis addresses learning without complete graph access.

Drawing on graph limit theory, the authors introduce a classification model that operates on a randomly sampled subgraph. They also define a topology for characterizing what the model can represent. This gives a mathematical language for asking which graph-level properties remain accessible through the model's partial observations.

The framework provides theoretical support for mini-batch learning on graphs and yields results on generalization bounds and transfer across graph sizes without assumptions on the input. The scope remains tied to representability: the title explicitly concerns estimating some graph parameters. The contribution explains how sampled local information can be sufficient for supported graph-level tasks, rather than claiming that every graph property is recoverable this way.
neurips-2021-learning-on-random-balls-is.tldr: A partial-observation framework explains when graph classification from randomly sampled subgraphs supports representation, generalization, and transfer across graph sizes.

paragraphs: Predictive checklists offer a simple form of clinical decision support: evaluate binary conditions and combine them with equal weights. This paper represents such checklists as discrete linear classifiers and learns them from data through integer programming. The formulation supports a search for globally optimal checklists within the chosen objective and constraints.

Users can impose complex requirements, including group-fairness constraints, and the method can turn real-valued measurements into binary features during training. It also associates learned models with an optimality gap. That gap indicates how much room for improvement remains relative to the optimization bound, helping guide model development and assess whether sufficiently accurate checklists are feasible.

Specialized techniques accelerate the search for checklists that perform well and have small optimality gaps. The authors evaluate the method on seven clinical classification problems and demonstrate a short checklist for PTSD screening. Their findings support the possibility of learning useful, simple decision aids while enforcing a rich set of application-specific requirements directly during training.
neurips-2021-learning-optimal-predictive.tldr: Integer programming learns simple predictive checklists with customizable constraints and optimality gaps that quantify remaining optimization uncertainty.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive semantic segmentation transfers pixel-labeling knowledge from labeled source images to an unlabeled target domain. Some approaches create target-like versions of source images as intermediate, or latent, domains. This paper uses those intermediate domains to explicitly connect multiple adaptation problems, rather than treating the translated images only as additional training data.

The method constructs pairs such as source-to-latent and latent-to-target. Under a meta-learning framework, knowledge about how to adapt one pair guides adaptation of another. The central idea is to transfer an adaptation strategy across domain pairs, making the relationships between domains part of the learning process.

The authors also address a target collection containing multiple domains without domain labels. An additional latent-to-latent pair helps reduce gaps involving the source and different latent domains, supporting simultaneous adaptation to multiple targets. On standard benchmarks, the method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches in both single-target and multiple-target settings. These results support learning across adaptation problems as a useful role for intermediate domains.
neurips-2021-learning-to-adapt-via-laten.tldr: The method learns how to adapt across intermediate domain pairs and uses that knowledge to improve single-target and multiple-target semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Online action detection must identify actions as video unfolds, making both recent motion and earlier context relevant. The Long Short-Term Transformer, or LSTR, models these two timescales with separate memory mechanisms. Its design gives extended history and fine-grained recent information distinct roles in the same temporal model.

The encoder dynamically uses coarse information from a long historical window. The abstract gives an example of 2,048 frames spanning up to eight minutes. The decoder focuses on fine-scale characteristics within a short window, illustrated by 32 frames spanning eight seconds. These are examples of the temporal windows, showing how the architecture combines prolonged context with detailed recent observations.

Extensive empirical analysis supports the authors' claim that LSTR models long videos effectively and efficiently with fewer heuristics than prior work. It achieves reported state-of-the-art results on THUMOS'14, TVSeries, and HACS Segment. The findings support separating temporal processing by scale as a practical way to use long video histories for online action detection.
neurips-2021-long-short-term-transformer.tldr: LSTR combines coarse long-term video memory with detailed short-term processing to achieve strong online action-detection results.

paragraphs: Relative entropy policy search, or REPS, has been used successfully for policy learning in simulated and real robotic domains. The paper addresses a gap between this practical use and theoretical understanding: what performance can be guaranteed when first-order, gradient-based methods optimize the REPS objective, particularly when gradients are stochastic?

The authors first analyze access to exact gradients. They show how getting close to the optimum of the optimization objective translates into getting close to an optimal policy. This link matters because progress on a mathematical training objective is useful only if it supports a corresponding statement about the learned decision-making policy.

They then study stochastic gradients and introduce an update technique that uses generative access to the underlying Markov decision process. Under that access setting, the updates maintain favorable convergence toward the optimal regularized policy. The contribution provides convergence rates and policy-suboptimality guarantees for these solvers, with the stochastic result explicitly relying on generative access and targeting the regularized optimum.
neurips-2021-near-optimal-policy-optimiz.tldr: The paper connects gradient-based optimization of REPS to policy-quality guarantees, including stochastic updates with generative access to the environment.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly breaks decision-making into single-step policies or models. This paper explores a sequence-based view: model states, actions, and rewards together, then use that representation to predict action sequences associated with high rewards. The approach brings Transformer sequence modeling to the structure of reinforcement learning trajectories.

The Transformer learns distributions over complete sequences of these quantities. In the proposed framework, the same sequence model fills roles that other approaches assign to separate components. The authors report that they do not need separate behavior-policy constraints commonly used in offline model-free learning, or ensembles and other epistemic-uncertainty estimators commonly used in model-based learning.

This consolidation simplifies a range of design decisions within their approach. Experiments demonstrate its flexibility across imitation learning, goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, and offline reinforcement learning. The stated finding is that one sequence-modeling formulation can support these different settings; the abstract does not claim a universal performance advantage. Its contribution is a unified way to represent and use the sequential structure of decision-making data.
neurips-2021-offline-reinforcement-learn.tldr: A Transformer models states, actions, and rewards jointly, providing a unified sequence-based approach across several reinforcement learning settings.

paragraphs: The paper asks when interacting with an environment improves imitation learning's statistical efficiency. Its analysis uses a recoverability assumption: at any state, action values under the expert policy are within mu of the maximum. This bounds how much the choice of action can change value when subsequent behavior follows the expert.

Under this assumption, an interactive algorithm achieves suboptimality scaling as mu times the number of states times horizon H, divided by N episodes, up to logarithmic factors. The authors show this is optimal to that precision. Offline learners using N expert trajectories still face a worst-case lower bound proportional to the number of states times H squared over N, establishing a separation in horizon dependence.

For experts represented by linear classifiers with known features, behavior cloning has a high-probability bound scaling as dH squared over N, up to logarithms. Sharing expert parameters across time improves this to dH over N. The paper also studies known transitions and introduces confidence-set linear classification as a tool for sample-efficient imitation learning.
neurips-2021-on-the-value-of-interaction.tldr: Under recoverability, interaction improves imitation learning's optimal horizon dependence, while linear expert structure and parameter sharing yield additional statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Federated learning participants may choose which other agents to collaborate with in order to reduce their own prediction errors. The paper studies this through a coalition game, asking how stable collaboration groups compare with groups chosen to minimize collective error. Stability and low average error are distinct objectives, so satisfying one need not automatically satisfy the other.

The authors define optimality using average error among participating agents and give an efficient algorithm for computing an optimal arrangement, with a correctness proof. They then identify regions of the parameter space where every stable arrangement is also optimal. In these regions, individual incentives and the collective error objective align.

That alignment does not hold everywhere: the paper supplies examples of stable arrangements with higher cost than the optimum. It nevertheless proves a constant upper bound on the gap. In the analyzed game, the worst stable arrangement has total error at most nine times that of an optimal arrangement. This quantifies the possible cost of stability without claiming stable groups always minimize error.
neurips-2021-optimality-and-stability-in.tldr: A coalition-game analysis computes optimal federations and bounds the worst stable arrangement's total error by nine times the optimum.

paragraphs: Private data analysis can become costly when data have many coordinates, even when their underlying variation occupies far fewer dimensions. This paper studies how to identify that smaller linear space while preserving differential privacy. The motivating distinction is between the dimension of the surrounding representation and the dimension of the structure actually present in the data.

The authors present algorithms for data sampled from a low-dimensional linear subspace, allowing a small amount of error in the input. The algorithms return the subspace itself or an approximation. Their task is therefore to recover useful geometric structure privately, including the case where observations lie only approximately within that structure.

The abstract highlights gradients in optimization as one setting where such low-dimensional structure can arise. Identifying it can avoid privacy or accuracy costs tied to the full ambient dimension. The proposed algorithms can serve as preprocessing for other procedures, making private structural recovery a preliminary step toward analysis that takes advantage of the data's lower-dimensional organization.
neurips-2021-privately-learning-subspace.tldr: Differentially private algorithms recover exact or approximate low-dimensional subspaces to help subsequent analysis avoid costs tied to ambient dimension.

paragraphs: Multiple-object tracking and segmentation combines detecting objects, maintaining their identities over time, and marking their pixels. Many approaches use temporal information to associate objects across frames while predicting each segmentation mask from a single frame. PCAN brings information from earlier frames into the segmentation process as well as the broader online tracking task.

The network compresses a space-time memory into a set of prototypes and uses cross-attention to retrieve information from past frames. For individual objects, an appearance module learns contrasting foreground and background prototypes. These representations are propagated over time, allowing the model to carry forward information about both the object and its surroundings.

The authors report that PCAN outperforms the compared video tracking and segmentation competition winners on Youtube-VIS and BDD100K. They also demonstrate effectiveness with both one-stage and two-stage segmentation frameworks. These findings support prototype-based temporal memory as a useful way to improve object masks and tracking together, with evidence across the two evaluated framework types.
neurips-2021-prototypical-cross-attentio.tldr: PCAN uses prototype-based temporal memory and cross-attention to improve online multiple-object tracking and segmentation.

paragraphs: A decision-making agent can face uncertainty because it does not know the environment and because the environment itself behaves randomly. This paper studies risk-averse learning in a Bayes-adaptive setting, where uncertainty about the environment is represented through a prior distribution over Markov decision processes. The objective is conditional value at risk, or CVaR, of total return.

CVaR focuses on the unfavorable portion of the return distribution. The authors show that optimizing it in this setting produces a policy that is risk-averse toward both uncertainty about which environment is present and inherent randomness within that environment. This connects one return-based objective to both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.

The authors reformulate the optimization problem as a two-player stochastic game and develop an approximate solution method combining Monte Carlo tree search with Bayesian optimization. Experiments show significant improvements over the baseline approaches evaluated for this problem. The contribution combines a characterization of what the risk objective covers with an approximate planning algorithm for pursuing that objective.
neurips-2021-risk-averse-bayes-adaptive-.tldr: Optimizing CVaR in Bayes-adaptive reinforcement learning accounts for both model uncertainty and environmental randomness through a risk-averse planning objective.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel describes infinitely wide neural networks trained with gradient descent under least-squares loss. Although kernel regression can perform well, its computational requirements make large learning problems difficult. This paper develops approximations intended to make neural tangent kernel methods practical at larger scales.

The authors sketch polynomial expansions of arc-cosine kernels, producing an NTK approximation with runtime near the input's sparsity scale. For the convolutional version, their sketch transforms an image in time linear in its pixel count. They also combine sketching with random features selected through leverage-score sampling to prove a spectral approximation guarantee for the NTK matrix.

The methods are evaluated on large regression and classification tasks. On CIFAR-10, a linear regressor trained on the approximate convolutional NTK features matches the accuracy of exact CNTK while achieving a reported 150-fold speedup. This result illustrates the practical value of approximating the kernel's feature representation, while the spectral guarantee supplies theoretical support for the matrix approximation.
neurips-2021-scaling-neural-tangent-kern.tldr: Sketching and random features accelerate neural tangent kernels, with a reported 150-fold speedup while matching exact CNTK accuracy on CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: A learned environment model lets a reinforcement learning agent plan using computation instead of collecting additional interactions. Planning can improve estimates of future value or the policy used to choose actions. This paper examines whether planning benefits from explicitly encouraging agreement between the learned model and the value function.

Classic approaches such as Dyna update the value function to agree with the model's predictions. The authors explore joint self-consistency, where the relationship between model and value is itself a learning target. This broadens the available updates beyond treating the model as the fixed reference that the value function must follow.

The paper proposes several possible self-consistency updates and evaluates them in both tabular settings and settings using function approximation. With appropriate choices, the authors find that these updates can help both policy evaluation and control. The qualification matters: the reported benefit depends on the update choice. The work identifies joint model-value consistency as a useful additional design direction for model-based reinforcement learning.
neurips-2021-self-consistent-models-and-.tldr: Appropriately chosen updates that encourage joint consistency between models and value functions can improve policy evaluation and control.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the conditions represented by training data. Some detection methods require examples of such inputs during training, which may be unavailable. This paper instead uses predictive normalized maximum likelihood, or pNML, without making assumptions about the tested input.

The authors derive an explicit pNML expression and its regret for a single-layer neural network. They show good generalization under either of two conditions: the test vector lies in the subspace associated with large eigenvalues of the training data's empirical correlation matrix, or the sample is far from the decision boundary. These are sufficient conditions, rather than a claim that other inputs cannot generalize.

The derived regret is applied efficiently to pretrained deep networks through their last layer followed by softmax. This application needs neither extra data nor additional tunable parameters. Across 74 OOD benchmarks involving the stated network architectures and datasets, the authors report improvements of up to 15.6% over recent leading methods, supporting the usefulness of the last-layer construction.
neurips-2021-single-layer-predictive-nor.tldr: A last-layer pNML regret measure enables OOD detection on pretrained networks without extra data or tunable parameters.

paragraphs: In node-level graph learning, examples are connected and need not be independent or identically distributed. This complicates understanding how a graph neural network will perform on unlabeled nodes. The paper develops a PAC-Bayesian analysis for a non-IID, semi-supervised setting, explicitly addressing this dependence rather than assuming ordinary independent examples.

The analysis considers different subgroups of unlabeled nodes instead of only an overall generalization measure. That makes it possible to study fairness through differences in predictive accuracy across groups. Under the paper's assumptions, distance between a test subgroup and the training set can be a key factor affecting performance on that subgroup.

This result draws attention to the selection of labeled training nodes: their relationship to different test groups can matter for accuracy disparities. Experiments across multiple graph neural network models and datasets support the theoretical results. The contribution supplies an assumption-dependent explanation for subgroup performance differences and a reason to consider training-node selection when designing fair graph-learning procedures.
neurips-2021-subgroup-generalization-and.tldr: A subgroup generalization analysis links GNN accuracy disparities to distance from the training set under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies the training dynamics of over-parameterized tensor decomposition under gradient flow. Empirically, this process often captures larger tensor components before finding smaller ones. That ordering resembles deflation, a decomposition strategy that recovers components progressively. The authors investigate when this observed pattern can be supported by a mathematical result.

For orthogonally decomposable tensors, they prove that a slightly modified gradient-flow procedure follows a deflation process and recovers every tensor component. Both the orthogonal structure and the modification to gradient flow belong to the stated result. The proof gives a precise setting in which progressive component discovery is more than an empirical observation.

The analysis suggests a connection to greedy low-rank learning in matrices: optimization dynamics can uncover structure in an ordered way even in an over-parameterized representation. The authors present this as a first step toward understanding implicit regularization for low-rank tensors. Its significance is the link between the path taken during training and the structured decomposition ultimately recovered.
neurips-2021-understanding-deflation-pro.tldr: For orthogonally decomposable tensors, a modified gradient flow provably recovers components through a deflation-like process.
